title: [WIP] TCP: Extend the SEQ analysis precedence preference
description:
Some packets remain recalcitrant to correct SEQ interpretation
(Retrans/Out-Of-Order) as OOO are never tested against ordinary
retransmissions.
The precedence preference is extended to ordinary retransmissions
then the user can reduce OOO packets and increase Retransmissions.
Closes #10725. Closes #17714.

notes.body: There are tests that test the out of order reassembly. Those tests manually turn on the TCP reassemble out of order preference. You need at the least to set your preference in several of the tests in [suite_dissection](test/suite_dissection.py) and [test/suite_clopts.py](test/suite_clopts.py). (The latter possibly you could change the expected output.)

Thanks, but .. no idea how to do that. Do we have at least a short introduction to that technology ?

edit : OK I see it's not that difficult and now it is passing the tests. Would you please @johnthacker have a look ?

Can you take a look at #13388 as well and see why this change doesn't fix that one?

In that case, there's a large number of out of order packets (but no retransmissions - or rather these are retransmissions where the missing packets were all lost), and reassembly works properly only with "Analyze Sequence Numbers" off. Even with this patch and the preference set to prefer OOO, it doesn't recognize them as being out of order. I assume it has something to do with the delay being larger than the calculated OOO threshold based on the other RTT.

There's a number of frames part of the reassembled frame 163 transmitted, then there's a gap of where after packet 90 there's initially missing data. TCP segments for later in frame 163 are received, followed by segments for what will be reassembled frame 169 are received. After frame 127 it goes back and starts sending missing segments. It fills in all but one of the holes for frame 163 in order, then goes back earlier and fills in the missing segment in frame 163, completing the reassembly, and then proceeds to transmit the last four frames for frame 169.
The answer may be that's a slightly different issue that needs to be another MR, just wanted to bring it to your attention either way.

I reckon it's a difference between reassembly's conception of retransmission vs out-of-order - "has this packet with non-consecutive sequence number appeared in the capture file before (retransmission) or is this the first time (out of order)?"

Whereas the definition in the sequence analysis as I understand it is closer to "was this originally _sent_ more than once (retransmission) or only once (out-of-order)?"

The difference is in packets that were probably from the sending host's point of view retransmissions but only appear once in the capture file because the original transmission was lost (and that is ultimately why they were retransmitted, and if the capture is closer to the receiving host network interface it's more likely to look like this.)

Indeed, if the sequence analysis is going to use that definition, then the reassembly code should _not_ rely on information from the sequence analysis and should do only its own tracking of segments that have appeared more than once (which is trickier for the rarer case of overlapping sequence numbers.)

I feel like !7424 is doing what I was expecting, but some feedback from people (Laura, Betty, Chris ?..) who are intensely investigating TCP stories would be welcome. Or some words during the DEV Den would also confirm from knowledgeable people.

An enhancement could be to replace the default values when we don't have the SYN-ACK sequences with something more realistic taken from the capture itself (based on RTT seen), but I would do that in another MR, if the idea is accepted.

#13388 took my time and I am suggesting something in !7543. Let's jump there to talk.
I'm not working on this MR anymore, the remaining issue will be addressed another way

@@ -693,9 +693,10 @@ Supersedes “TCP Dup ACK”.
 ==== TCP Ambiguous Interpretations
 
 Some captures are quite difficult to analyze automatically, particularly when the
-time frame may cover both Fast Retransmission and Out-Of-Order packets. A TCP
-preference allows to switch the precedence of these two interpretations at the
-protocol level.
+time frame may cover two or three cases and be interpreted as Retransmission,
+Fast Retransmission and Out-Of-Order packets. The TCP protocol preference
+“Retransmissions preferred over Out-of-Order interpretation” (enabled by default)
+allows to switch the interpretation precedence at the protocol level.
 
 // TCP_A_CONVERSATION_COMPLETENESS
 [discrete]
